notebooks.title: Conceptual Frameworks for Autonomous AI Discovery
notebooks.summary: This revision synthesizes strategies for autonomous problem identification by contrasting routine task performance with frameworks like VALID, which emphasize biological grounding and artifact control to ensure genuine research novelty.
notebooks.findings:
Significant research problems in AI require rigorous evaluation criteria beyond simple metric optimization to avoid the 'doppelgänger effect' where test data mimics training data. [source-b0e8eca8af634a57]

Distinguishing significant problems from routine ones in an autonomous context requires criteria such as 'veracious biological grounding' and 'deployment-aware performance'. [source-b0e8eca8af634a57]
notebooks.limitations: Current evidence focuses on computational biology; extrapolation to general scientific domains remains a hypothesis.
notebooks.next_questions: How can the VALID framework's principles be generalized to non-biological domains of autonomous scientific discovery?

notebooks.title: Rational Responses to Epistemic Peer Disagreement
notebooks.summary: Epistemic disagreement occurs when agents with identical evidence reach different conclusions. The literature identifies three primary stances: the Conciliatory view, the Stubborn view, and the Non-Conciliatory view. These stances interact with Uniqueness and Permissivism; Uniqueness asserts that evidence dictates one correct rational attitude, whereas Permissivism allows for multiple. Current evidence suggests that unconditional deference (Conciliatory view) may be less tenable than a nuanced approach that accounts for case-specific conditions.
notebooks.findings: There is no single consensus on whether rational agents should defer to epistemic peers in all cases of disagreement. [source-8259eb518d4a419c]
notebooks.limitations: The current evidence is limited to a single thesis overview of philosophical positions. Computational or algorithmic implementations of these positions in AI agents remain unexamined.
notebooks.next_questions: How do these philosophical positions map to specific consensus-seeking algorithms in multi-agent systems? Are there objective metrics to determine when a 'peer' is actually an epistemic equal?
notebooks.reason: This notebook synthesizes the initial source material into a structured assessment of the project's core philosophical question.

claims.statement: There is no single consensus on whether rational agents should defer to epistemic peers in all cases of disagreement.

support.explanation: The source explicitly identifies the lack of consensus by outlining three distinct theoretical responses to disagreement.
support.passage: In the current debate of the epistemology of peer disagreement, it is controversial whether one is rationally required to suspend one’s judgment when disputing with peers. Three different views have been proposed: (1) The Conciliatory view: we should always move at least a bit in the direction of the epistemic peer’s. (2) The Stubborn view: we should always not be moved by peer disagreement. (3) The Non-Conciliatory view: in some cases of peer disagreement we should be moved by peer disagreement, but in some cases of peer disagreement we should not be moved by peer disagreement.

nodes.title: Rational Responses to Epistemic Peer Disagreement

detail.title: Rational Responses to Epistemic Peer Disagreement
detail.summary: Epistemic disagreement occurs when agents with identical evidence reach different conclusions. The literature identifies three primary stances: the Conciliatory view, the Stubborn view, and the Non-Conciliatory view. These stances interact with Uniqueness and Permissivism; Uniqueness asserts that evidence dictates one correct rational attitude, whereas Permissivism allows for multiple. Current evidence suggests that unconditional deference (Conciliatory view) may be less tenable than a nuanced approach that accounts for case-specific conditions.
detail.findings: There is no single consensus on whether rational agents should defer to epistemic peers in all cases of disagreement. [source-8259eb518d4a419c]
detail.limitations: The current evidence is limited to a single thesis overview of philosophical positions. Computational or algorithmic implementations of these positions in AI agents remain unexamined.
detail.next_questions: How do these philosophical positions map to specific consensus-seeking algorithms in multi-agent systems? Are there objective metrics to determine when a 'peer' is actually an epistemic equal?
detail.reason: This notebook synthesizes the initial source material into a structured assessment of the project's core philosophical question.

review.alternative: A consensus might exist that the source does not discuss.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of a widely accepted formal proof or standardized algorithm that mandates one specific response to peer disagreement.

claims.statement: There is no single consensus on whether rational agents should defer to epistemic peers in all cases of disagreement.

support.explanation: The source explicitly identifies the lack of consensus by outlining three distinct theoretical responses to disagreement.
support.passage: In the current debate of the epistemology of peer disagreement, it is controversial whether one is rationally required to suspend one’s judgment when disputing with peers. Three different views have been proposed: (1) The Conciliatory view: we should always move at least a bit in the direction of the epistemic peer’s. (2) The Stubborn view: we should always not be moved by peer disagreement. (3) The Non-Conciliatory view: in some cases of peer disagreement we should be moved by peer disagreement, but in some cases of peer disagreement we should not be moved by peer disagreement.

support_provenance.statement: There is no single consensus on whether rational agents should defer to epistemic peers in all cases of disagreement.

nodes.title: Conceptual Frameworks for Autonomous AI Discovery

detail.title: Conceptual Frameworks for Autonomous AI Discovery
detail.summary: This revision synthesizes strategies for autonomous problem identification by contrasting routine task performance with frameworks like VALID, which emphasize biological grounding and artifact control to ensure genuine research novelty.
detail.findings:
Significant research problems in AI require rigorous evaluation criteria beyond simple metric optimization to avoid the 'doppelgänger effect' where test data mimics training data. [source-b0e8eca8af634a57]

Distinguishing significant problems from routine ones in an autonomous context requires criteria such as 'veracious biological grounding' and 'deployment-aware performance'. [source-b0e8eca8af634a57]
detail.limitations: Current evidence focuses on computational biology; extrapolation to general scientific domains remains a hypothesis.
detail.next_questions: How can the VALID framework's principles be generalized to non-biological domains of autonomous scientific discovery?
detail.reason: Notebook revision required to synthesize new collected evidence on rigor and problem identification.
